title: Early Quran Manuscripts: What the Physical Evidence Shows
subtitle: Physical witnesses to an early text, including what dates and variants cannot establish
summary: Early Quran manuscripts provide physical evidence for the antiquity and continuity of the Uthmanic written tradition. Birmingham's parchment dating, shared spelling patterns, regional variants, and the Sana'a palimpsest answer different questions. Together they support early stabilization, not an exact ink date or the claim that every early copy was identical.

seo.metaTitle: Early Quran Manuscripts: Birmingham, Sanaa, Samarkand Explained
seo.metaDescription: What Birmingham, regional codices, and Sana'a show about the Quran, with clear limits on dating, coverage, ownership, and textual uniformity.

sections.title: What a Leaf Can Tell You
sections.body:
An early manuscript can show that a passage or written form existed near Islam's beginnings. Comparing many copies can reveal common ancestry. Neither finding proves divine authorship or supplies the missing parts of a fragment.

The Quran's manuscript record is strong evidence against wholesale late invention of the familiar text. Its strength is clearer when actual variation is included in the account rather than hidden.

sections.title: Three Dates That Should Not Be Confused
sections.body:
Radiocarbon testing dates the material sampled. For parchment, it estimates when the animal died. Script analysis estimates when a style of writing was used. Textual comparison asks where the copy belongs in a tradition.

These methods can reinforce one another, but they do not produce a magically exact date for ink. A wide calibrated range is not evidence that every year inside it is equally likely, or that a Quran existed before Muhammad because the earliest endpoint precedes his life.

sections.title: Birmingham: Early Parchment, Partial Text
sections.body:
The [University of Birmingham's research account](https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/facilities/cadbury/birmingham-quran-mingana-collection/birmingham-quran/research-and-conservation) reports parchment dated to 568–645 CE at 95.4 percent probability. The leaves preserve portions of surahs 18–20. The ink has not been age-tested.

Quran 85:21–22 speaks of a Preserved Slate, while 15:9 promises protection. A laboratory does not test that heavenly claim. Muslims can see the physical evidence as consistent with preservation without converting the parchment range into proof of the entire theological account.

sections.title: A Fair Biblical Comparison
sections.body:
[Codex Sinaiticus](https://codexsinaiticus.org/en/codex/default.aspx), conventionally dated to the fourth century, preserves a complete New Testament; earlier New Testament fragments also exist. The relevant comparison is the interval from a work's origin, the amount preserved, and the relationships among witnesses.

A few Quran leaves and a complete New Testament do not answer the same coverage question. Nor is an object less useful because it is Christian. Good comparative work credits each witness for what it actually preserves.

sections.title: The Most Important Pattern Is Shared Ancestry
sections.body:
Repeated, unusual spellings across early Quran copies support a common written source, as [van Putten's study](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0041977X19000338) argues. [Regional manuscript analysis](https://www.lockwoodonlinejournals.com/index.php/jiqsa/article/view/554) also identifies limited differences among branches.

The inference is not that copyists made no mistakes. It is that the dominant tradition descends from an early written standard. This materially strengthens the traditional account of early standardization without proving every later report about its administration.

sections.title: Sana'a Is Evidence, Not an Embarrassment to Hide
sections.body:
A palimpsest is reused writing material: an earlier text was erased and another written above it. The Sana'a lower text contains genuine differences from the Uthmanic standard; [Sadeghi and Goudarzi's edition](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/san%C4%81-1-and-the-origins-of-the-qur%C4%81n/) treats it as evidence of an early nonstandard textual tradition. Its precise reconstruction and setting are debated.

That is a serious qualification to 'every copy always matched.' It does not show that the received Quran was created centuries later. Both early variation and early dominance of a standard can be true.

sections.title: What About Codices Attributed to Uthman?
sections.body:
A famous ownership tradition is not a chain of documented provenance. A codex should not be called Uthman's personal copy simply because it is revered under that name. Its script, material, and textual features must be assessed separately.

The preservation case does not need a museum to possess his own handwriting. It rests on the relationship among many early witnesses and the received tradition. That is a more durable argument than relying on an unverified relic attribution.

sections.title: The Conclusion the Evidence Warrants
sections.body:
We have strong physical evidence for an early common Quranic written tradition, together with real variation that needs explanation. Muslims regard this as consistent with divine protection; divine authorship is not a laboratory result.

Read [Uthmanic Standardization](/articles/uthmanic-standardization) to connect the manuscripts with the traditional history, and [Qira'at Explained Simply](/articles/qiraat-explained-simply) to understand what sparse early writing leaves to learned recitation.

sections.title: Inspect Before Repeating a Claim
sections.body: Use the holding institution for an object's description and dating, and research editions for textual comparisons. The studies below address different questions; none should be made to prove more than its evidence covers.

faq.question: Is Birmingham certainly the oldest Quran?
faq.answer: It is an important early fragment, not a securely dated complete Quran. Overlapping ranges and different dating methods make a single 'oldest' label uncertain.

faq.question: Did the radiocarbon test date the ink?
faq.answer: No. It dated the parchment material. Script and textual analysis supply additional evidence about the written object.

faq.question: Does the Sana'a lower text contain actual variants?
faq.answer: Yes. It should not be reduced to spelling variation alone. Its reconstruction and relationship to early codices remain scholarly questions.

faq.question: Do early manuscripts prove revelation?
faq.answer: No. They establish the history of the available text. The case that the message is from God needs further theological and historical reasoning.

faq.question: Must Uthman's own copy survive for preservation to be credible?
faq.answer: No. Common ancestry can be investigated through descendants even when a particular original is lost. Claims about personal ownership require separate provenance.
